newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon denies TV report on secret Bosnia force.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon denies TV report on secret Bosnia force.

text.p: The U.S. Defence Department on Tuesday denied a television report that a secret force of U.S., British and French military commandos was training to capture and arrest indicted Bosnian war criminals.

"Contrary to what has been reported this evening, U.S. forces are not now training for or participating in any unilateral or multilateral commando operation to apprehend indicted war criminals in the former Yugoslavia," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said.
"It is the policy of the administration to help the International War Crimes Tribunal to bring indicted war crininals to justice," he said.

Bacon declined to comment further on a report on ABC Television's "World News Tonight" programme that quoted U.S. military sources as saying a secret commando unit was training in Europe with the support of at least six other countries. The operation was separate from NATO peacekeeping, the report said.

ABC said the top two targets of the operation were former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic and military chief Gen. Ratko Mladic, who are wanted by an international war crimes tribunal but have shown their political clout by continuing to appear in public.

The sources told ABC that no political decision had been made to use the force, which had been trained in covert rescue and capture techniques, but that a general target date had been set for late autumn.
The network said the secret effort included intensified intelligence gathering by the Central Intelligence Agency plus covert surveillance by soldiers.
Bacon told reporters earlier on Tuesday that Washington continued to believe that arresting war criminals was "a police function" and not a job for the military.
He said the United States remained committed to aiding the war crimes tribunal but felt that capturing the indicted individuals was the "job of the former warring factions."
